newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dragonair cash to underpin profit.
newsitem.headline: Dragonair cash to underpin profit.

text.p: After a sometimes turbulent year, Hong Kong carrier Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd is expected to post an earnings result that relies heavily on one-off profits from the sale of much of Dragonair, analysts said.
Hong Kong's flag carrier exceeded expectations last year, posting a 24.7 percent profit rise, well ahead of the consensus forecast of 18 percent.

But this seems unlikely in the year to December 1996, which analysts said would be helped by the approximately HK$541 million gained from the disposal of most of its stake in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd (Dragonair) last April.
Analysts estimates of attributable profits, including the cash from the Dragonair deal, ranged from HK$3.7 billion, which would be up 24.2 percent from 1995, to HK$4.002 billion, up 34.4 percent.
With Dragonair stripped out, profit forecasts ranged between six percent and 16 percent.
Cathay Pacific's main shareholders are Swire Pacific Ltd with 43.86 percent, and red chip CITIC Pacific Ltd with 25 percent.

Dragonair's main shareholder is now state-owned China National Aviation Corp, which last April bought 17.66 percent from Swire and Cathay Pacific, and another 17.66 percent from CITIC Pacific, diluting CITIC's stake to about 28 percent.
Dragonair contributed HK$267 million to pre-tax profits in 1995, and would contribute HK$184 million in 1996, said Steven Thompson from the Nikko Research Center.
Analysts said Cathay Pacific faced factors beyond its control in 1996.
Higher fuel prices and a weaker yen had eaten into earnings. In contrast, the strong yen in 1995 helped Cathay Pacific's North Asian revenues.
"It was hit severely by macro factors, fuel and currency," said Mark Simpson of ING Barings. Fuel represented 16 percent of the carrier's total cost base, he said.
K.Y. Ng of BZW Asia said 1996 could be summed up as "a tough year for Cathay due to factors beyond their control." He also cited fuel and exchange rates.

Thompson said he was unaware of what Cathay Pacific paid for fuel in 1996, but noted the average price of aviation fuel had risen 21 percent to US$25.38 a barrel, compared with US$20.93 a barrel in 1995.
Simpson said passenger yields for 1996 were likely to be down 3.7 percent from 1995 levels, while cargo yields would be down five percent.
Simpson is forecasting attributable profits of HK$3.715 billion for 1996, up 24.7 percent on 1995 including the Dragonair sale, but up only 6.6 percent excluding Dragonair.
He expected overall earnings per share to rise 9.6 percent to HK$1.14 on 1995. When Dragonair is stripped out, he saw EPS at HK$0.98, down six percent.
Ng forecast an attributable profit of HK$3.78 billion, and another analyst, who declined to be named, expected attributable profits of HK$3.7 billion.
Nikko Research Center's Thompson expected attributable profits of HK$4.002 billion. He said he was more upbeat than most.
"I've heard so much negative comment on Cathay, (but) I'm pretty bullish," Thompson said.
